# The design limits the questions: identification {#sec-identification}

In the north of the Netherlands, decades of gas extraction have caused earthquakes, and the people who live above the gas field vote differently from the rest of the country. Researchers who surveyed the region proposed a chain of explanations [@otjes2020]: experiencing earthquakes erodes trust in the national government, feeds a sense of injustice, and strengthens regional identification, and each of these in turn pushes people toward a protest vote. @fig-otjes draws the claim, and the drawing shows its shape. The theory does not stop at "earthquakes cause protest voting"; it says the effect runs *through* something. Questions of this shape are called **mediation** questions, and the social and health sciences ask them constantly, because a mechanism is what a theory is made of, and because a mediator suggests a lever: if distrust carries the effect, restoring trust might interrupt it.

![The protest-voting theory of @otjes2020 as a path diagram: earthquake experience works on the protest vote through several parallel mediators.](diagrams/otjes.png){#fig-otjes width="85%" fig-align="center"}

Mediation can be used to illustrate a larger predicament, and that predicament is my real subject. The last chapter warned that a model which fits the data is not thereby true. Here you meet the hard version of the warning: some questions cannot be settled by any amount of data, because the design never put the answer into the data in the first place. Statisticians call this the problem of "identification". Identification is a limit on knowledge, in which the design, not the sample size, sets the limit.

## The cross-sectional mediation model

The recipe of @sec-theory-to-glm turns the simplest mediation theory into two equations. In the notation of that chapter, the cause is exogenous, so it is written $\xi$; the mediator and the outcome are endogenous, $\eta_1$ and $\eta_2$. With all three variables standardized:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\eta_1 &= \gamma_1\,\xi + \zeta_1 \\
\eta_2 &= \beta\,\eta_1 + \gamma_2\,\xi + \zeta_2 .
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-mediation}

This is exactly the practice model of @sec-theory-to-glm, and the decomposition rule gives the property that makes mediation attractive. Two relationships connect $\xi$ and $\eta_2$: the direct effect, which contributes $\gamma_2$, and an indirect effect through the mediator, which contributes $\gamma_1 \beta$. Their sum is the total effect, and here, only because nothing in this model is a common cause of $\xi$ and $\eta_2$, that sum is also the implied correlation. Estimating the two equations and multiplying yields "the share of the effect that runs through the mediator".^[This estimation recipe has circulated in psychology for decades under the name of @baron1986. My subject is what the numbers mean, not how to compute them.]

::: {.callout-tip icon="false" title="Exercise 3.1"}
In a study of education ($\xi$), health knowledge ($\eta_1$), and longevity ($\eta_2$), the estimates are $\hat\gamma_1 = 0.5$, $\hat\beta = 0.4$, $\hat\gamma_2 = 0.1$. Compute the indirect, direct, and total effects and the proportion mediated. Then state in one sentence what the indirect effect claims about the world, if the model is true.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false" title="Answer 3.1"}
Indirect $= 0.5 \times 0.4 = 0.20$; direct $= 0.10$; total $= 0.30$; proportion mediated $= 0.20/0.30 = 2/3$. The claim: two thirds of education's benefit for longevity arises because education raises health knowledge, which raises longevity, so an intervention on health knowledge alone could capture most of the benefit. That is a very strong claim. Everything that follows asks what entitles anyone to it.
:::

## The assumptions behind the arrows

Equations [-@eq-mediation] are claims, and by now you know where claims get their credibility. To read $\hat\gamma_1$, $\hat\beta$, and $\hat\gamma_2$ causally you must grant, beyond linearity and additivity: that nothing confounds the cause and the mediator; that nothing confounds the mediator and the outcome, which is to say that $\zeta_1$ and $\zeta_2$ are uncorrelated; and that the arrows point the way drawn.

Here is mediation's trap. Randomizing $\xi$, the strongest design feature we own, secures the first assumption outright, because a coin flip shares no common causes with anything. It secures nothing for the other two. Nobody randomized the mediator. Within each arm of a randomized experiment, the people with high mediator values are simply different people from the people with low values, and whatever makes them different may drive the outcome on its own. The $\beta$ path is an observational study inside the experiment. Methodologists have said so plainly for years: the mediator-outcome assumption "is needed even in the randomized trial context because, in a trial, although the exposure has been randomized, the mediator typically has not been" [@vanderweele2016]. In one randomized trial of cognitive behavioral therapy, a naive mediation analysis of antidepressant use made the antidepressants look harmful; VanderWeele's verdict is that "we get nonsense from the traditional approach if we ignore mediator-outcome confounding".

The next two sections show these failures happening in simulated data, where the truth is known and the failure can be watched directly.

## Failure one: the arrows can be backwards

The first simulation builds a world in which the mediation model is exactly true: the cause raises the mediator ($\gamma_1 = 0.5$), the mediator raises the outcome ($\beta = 0.7$), and no direct effect exists. Two models are then fitted to this world: the true chain, and the same chain with every arrow reversed.

```{r}
#| label: reversed-arrows
library(lavaan)
set.seed(21)
n  <- 10000
x1 <- rnorm(n)
x2 <- 0.5 * x1 + rnorm(n)
x3 <- 0.7 * x2 + rnorm(n)
d  <- data.frame(x1, x2, x3)

fit_chain    <- sem("x2 ~ x1 \n x3 ~ x2", data = d)
fit_reversed <- sem("x1 ~ x2 \n x2 ~ x3", data = d)
c(chain = fitMeasures(fit_chain, "chisq"),
  reversed = fitMeasures(fit_reversed, "chisq"))
```

The simulation builds the world; the two `sem()` calls fit the rival stories; the last line prints their fit statistics. The statistics agree to every decimal, in this dataset and in every dataset either model will ever meet.

::: {.callout-tip icon="false" title="Exercise 3.2"}
(a) Change the two parameter values in the simulation above (for example, replace 0.5 and 0.7 by values of your own), rerun the code, and compare the two chi-square statistics. What changes, and what does not?
(b) Explain the result using the decomposition rule. What does each model imply about the three correlations among $x_1$, $x_2$, $x_3$?
(c) Then check a third story: fit the model in which $x_3$ causes both $x_1$ and $x_2$ (`"x1 ~ x3 \n x2 ~ x3"`). Does it also fit identically? Why (not)?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false" title="Answer 3.2"}
(a) The chi-square values change, because they depend on the simulated data. But the two models' chi-squares remain identical to every decimal, whatever values you choose. The equivalence is a property of the two *models*, not of particular parameter values: for every dataset, each model can fit exactly as well as the other.
(b) Both chains imply the same single restriction. The forward chain implies $\rho_{13} = \rho_{12}\,\rho_{23}$, since the only relationship between $x_1$ and $x_3$ is the indirect effect through $x_2$; the reversed chain implies $\rho_{13} = \rho_{23}\,\rho_{12}$, the same equation. Models that imply identical restrictions on the observable correlations cannot be told apart by any data.
(c) The common-cause story is different: it implies $\rho_{12} = \rho_{13}\,\rho_{23}$, a restriction that is false in this world, so its fit is visibly worse. Fit can eliminate some rivals; it cannot orient the chain.^[For the curious: with nonlinear relationships or non-normal variables the tie can sometimes be broken, because a reversed nonlinear relationship leaves distributional fingerprints. Under linearity and normality the equivalence is exact.]
:::

This situation has a name. Two models, or two parameter values, are **equivalent** when they imply the same distribution of observable data. The question of which of two equivalent models or parameter values is correct is then not **identified**: the data have no opinion, however many of them you collect. A model with more parameters than observed variances and covariances cannot possibly be identified. But the counting rule is only a necessary condition, and the reversed chain passes it while the direction stays unidentifiable all the same. Design can break the tie that fit cannot. If $x_1$ was randomized, an arrow into $x_1$ is absurd, because nothing in the system causes a coin flip; the reversed chain is ruled out by design, not by fit. The earthquake study leans on the same logic in weaker form: earthquakes shake houses, and opinions do not shake the ground, so the causal order of the exposure is secure. For the mediator-outcome pair, nothing is secure. Distrust may drive protest votes, or a protest identity may feed distrust, and the survey cannot tell.

## Failure two: the hidden confounder

Now the second assumption. In a new world, the cause still raises the mediator ($\gamma_1 = 0.5$), but the mediator does nothing whatsoever to the outcome. An unmeasured variable $U$ drives both mediator and outcome instead. Picture a randomized encouragement to study ($X$), study time ($M$), test scores ($Y$), and conscientiousness ($U$).

```{r}
#| label: hidden-confounder
set.seed(5)
n <- 10000
X <- rnorm(n)
U <- rnorm(n) # never measured
M <- 0.5 * X + 0.6 * U + rnorm(n, sd = sqrt(1 - 0.25 - 0.36))
Y <- 0.0 * M + 0.6 * U + rnorm(n, sd = sqrt(1 - 0.36))
d2 <- data.frame(X, M, Y) # does not include U  :(

round(coef(sem("M ~ X \n Y ~ M + X", data = d2)), 2)
```

The mediation analysis reports a highly significant $\hat\beta$ of about 0.5, which a reader might take as evidence that studying strongly improves scores and that the encouragement works through study time. Every number is precisely estimated, and every causal number is wrong: in this world, forcing students to study more would achieve nothing, because study time does not cause scores. Conscientiousness merely makes the two travel together inside each arm of the experiment. Notice the estimated direct effect too, pushed spuriously *negative*. More data would only tighten the intervals around the wrong values. This is @fig-confounding again, with one difference that matters. There the confounded variable was the treatment, and randomization fixed it. Here the confounded variable is the mediator, and randomization cannot reach it.

::: {.callout-tip icon="false" title="Exercise 3.3"}
Explain, with a trace through the diagram $X \rightarrow M \leftarrow U \rightarrow Y$, why the regression of $Y$ on $M$ and $X$ produces a nonzero coefficient on $M$ although $M$ does not cause $Y$. Then explain why randomizing $X$ did not protect us.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false" title="Answer 3.3"}
$M$ and $Y$ share the common cause $U$: high-$U$ students study more and also score higher, so $M$ and $Y$ are correlated at every level of $X$. Regression can only redescribe that correlation, and it attributes the association to the $M$ coefficient. In model terms, $U$ sits inside both $\zeta_1$ and $\zeta_2$, so the disturbances are correlated, violating the no-confounding assumption. Randomization guarantees that $U$ is unrelated to $X$, which is why $\hat a$ and the total effect remain fine. It constrains nothing about $U$'s relation to $M$ or $Y$. The coin flip protects only the variable it assigned.
:::

## Trading one assumption for another: instrumental variables

If we believe there is unmeasured confounding, then this belief should be reflected in the model, as a correlation between the disturbance terms.

With a direct path from $\xi$ to $\eta_2$ still in the model, the unknowns are $\gamma_1$, $\beta$, $\gamma_2$, and the disturbance correlation $\psi$: four parameters facing three observable correlations. One short; not identified, and this time the counting rule alone settles it. But suppose the theory can credibly assert that there is *no direct path*, that $\xi$ reaches $\eta_2$ only through $\eta_1$. @fig-iv draws that model. The parameters now number three, and the decomposition rule gives three equations:

![The confounded mediation model. The curved arrow between the disturbances represents unmeasured common causes of mediator and outcome. There is no direct path from the cause to the outcome.](diagrams/mediation.png){#fig-iv width="70%" fig-align="center"}

$$
\rho_{\xi\eta_1} = \gamma_1, \qquad
\rho_{\eta_1\eta_2} = \beta + \psi\text{-term}, \qquad
\rho_{\xi\eta_2} = \gamma_1\,\beta .
$$

The middle equation says the naive mediator-outcome correlation is contaminated: it contains $\beta$ plus a contribution from the correlated disturbances. The other two equations do not contain $\psi$ at all, because no relationship between $\xi$ and either endogenous variable runs through the curved arrow. So we can solve for the target of interest, $\beta$, by dividing the third equation by the first:

$$
\beta = \frac{\rho_{\xi\eta_2}}{\rho_{\xi\eta_1}} .
$$

The causal effect of the mediator is identified *without assuming away the confounding*; $\psi$ has become just another parameter for the data to estimate. In plain terms, the assumption "no mediator-outcome confounding" has been traded for the assumption "no direct effect", which in this role is called the **exclusion restriction**. Neither assumption is testable from these data; the trade rests entirely on theory. When the theory is credible, $\xi$ is called an **instrumental variable** [@angrist1996]: it is no longer of interest for its own sake, but because its randomness moves the mediator, which makes the mediator's effect on the outcome visible.

Applied to the very dataset that misled the mediation analysis:

```{r}
#| label: iv-estimate
model_iv <- "
  M ~ a * X
  Y ~ b * M
  M ~~ Y        # correlated disturbances: confounding allowed
"
round(coef(sem(model_iv, data = d2))[c("a", "b")], 2)
round(cov(d2$X, d2$Y) / cov(d2$X, d2$M), 2)   # the same, by hand
```

The estimate recovers the truth: studying does nothing, correctly reported, from confounded data. And the second line shows that the estimator is a single division.

@sec-rq-to-interpretation already did this division by hand. The Oregon arithmetic, where an effect on those drawn in the lottery was divided by a 25-point rise in coverage, is the same ratio $\rho_{\xi\eta_2}/\rho_{\xi\eta_1}$ in a different notation. The numerator has a name of its own, the **intention-to-treat** effect, and the assumption that licensed the division was the exclusion restriction all along.

It is worth doing the algebra once with pure numbers. Suppose we observe $\rho_{\xi\eta_1} = 0.3$, $\rho_{\eta_1\eta_2} = 0.7$, and $\rho_{\xi\eta_2} = 0.15$. The instrumental-variable estimate is $\beta = 0.15/0.3 = 0.5$. The naive estimate, the raw mediator-outcome correlation, is $0.7$. The difference, $0.2$, is confounding that the naive analysis counted as causation.

The estimator depends on three conditions. Each of them fails regularly in practice, so each deserves to be spelled out.

*Relevance.* The recipe divides by $\rho_{\xi\eta_1} = \gamma_1$. If the instrument barely moves the mediator, the division amplifies noise; if $\gamma_1 = 0$, there is nothing to divide by at all. Weak instruments do not merely widen intervals; they make the estimator erratic, as the next exercise shows, and, when the instrument is even slightly invalid, badly biased [@bound1995].

::: {.callout-tip icon="false" title="Exercise 3.4"}
The function below simulates one instrumental-variable study with $n = 1{,}000$, in a world where the true effect of the mediator is zero, and returns the IV estimate. The argument `g1` is the strength of the instrument.

```{r}
#| label: weak-instrument-setup
one_iv <- function(g1) {
  U <- rnorm(1000)
  X <- rnorm(1000)
  M <- g1 * X + 0.6 * U + rnorm(1000)
  Y <- 0.6 * U + rnorm(1000)     # the true effect of M on Y is zero
  cov(X, Y) / cov(X, M)
}
```

(a) Run `replicate(500, one_iv(0.5))` to simulate 500 studies with a strong instrument, and look at the estimates with `summary()`. Around which value do they concentrate, and how far out do the most extreme estimates lie?
(b) Do the same with a weak instrument, `one_iv(0.05)`. Compare the two summaries.
(c) Explain what the division by `cov(X, M)` has to do with the difference.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false" title="Answer 3.4"}
(a) The strong-instrument estimates concentrate tightly around the true value 0; across 500 studies they typically stay within about $\pm 0.2$.
(b) The weak-instrument estimates are wild: most lie further from zero than the *worst* strong-instrument estimate, more than a quarter lie beyond $\pm 1$, and individual studies can return estimates in the tens, of either sign.
(c) The IV estimate divides by the sample covariance between instrument and mediator. With `g1 = 0.05` the true covariance is barely different from zero, so in any one sample the estimated covariance can come out close to zero, or on the wrong side of it, and dividing by a near-zero number produces an estimate that is huge and of unpredictable sign. The information about $\beta$ that the instrument carries shrinks with $\gamma_1$, and at $\gamma_1 = 0$ it is gone entirely.
:::

*Exclusion.* The restriction "no direct path" did real work in the algebra: it removed the direct effect from $\rho_{\xi\eta_2}$, leaving only $\gamma_1\beta$. If a direct path exists after all, the numerator contains $\gamma_1\beta + \gamma_2$, and the ratio silently delivers a corrupted answer. The data cannot check this, because the model with the direct path was never identified in the first place.

*Exogeneity.* And $\xi$ itself must be unconfounded with the outcome, which randomization guarantees and nature sometimes imitates.

::: {.callout-tip icon="false" title="Exercise 3.5"}
Work through the full identification argument yourself, in the steps the algebra suggests. (a) Using the decomposition rule on @fig-iv, write the three implied correlations in terms of $\gamma_1$, $\beta$, and $\psi$. (Hint: the joint-effect contribution to $\rho_{\eta_1\eta_2}$ that uses the curved arrow may be written simply as "$+$ confounding".) (b) Which two equations identify $\beta$, and why is the third not needed? (c) What goes wrong if we never observed $\xi$ and wanted $\beta$ from the mediator-outcome data alone? (d) What goes wrong if $\gamma_1 = 0$?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false" title="Answer 3.5"}
(a) $\rho_{\xi\eta_1} = \gamma_1$; $\rho_{\xi\eta_2} = \gamma_1\beta$; $\rho_{\eta_1\eta_2} = \beta + \text{confounding}$. (b) The first two: $\beta = \rho_{\xi\eta_2}/\rho_{\xi\eta_1}$. They are exactly the equations free of $\psi$. The third equation is then left over to *estimate* the confounding rather than to assume it away. (c) With only the mediator and the outcome you have one correlation and two unknowns, $\beta$ and the confounding; not identified, which is the ordinary observational predicament. (d) Division by zero: with an irrelevant instrument the data contain no information about $\beta$, and in finite samples a nearly-zero $\gamma_1$ produces the wild estimates of Exercise 3.4.
:::

## Instruments in the wild

Where do credible instruments come from? Sometimes nature provides one. @hanandita2014 wanted the effect of poverty on mental health in Indonesia, where the naive association is hopelessly confounded: illness causes poverty too, and much causes both. Their instrument is the weather. Rainfall anomalies across 440 districts shift household consumption, and a rainfall shock has no business affecting mental health except through the economic hardship it causes. With $N = 577{,}548$, relevance is checkable and strong, exogeneity is argued from meteorology, and the exclusion restriction is the debatable clause, as it always is.^[Is it airtight? Floods can destroy more than income: homes, and occasionally family members, are direct paths from rainfall to distress that bypass consumption. Every instrumental-variable argument has a clause like this, and the paper's robustness checks are aimed at it.] Their estimate: halving consumption raises the probability of mental illness by 0.06, about five times the naive association, which measurement error in consumption had attenuated.

Sometimes we build the instrument. An **encouragement design** randomizes not the behaviour itself but an invitation to it, then uses the randomized invitation as an instrument for the behaviour [@holland1988]. The same logic runs any trial with imperfect compliance: assignment is randomized, treatment received is not, and assignment instruments treatment received. In the JOBS II trial for unemployed workers, only some of those assigned to job-search workshops attended, so assignment served as the instrument for participation [@tingley2014].

And sometimes biology randomizes. **Mendelian randomization** uses genetic variants as instruments: a variant that raises alcohol consumption is dealt out at conception, plausibly independent of later confounders, and instruments the effect of drinking on, say, esophageal cancer [@daveysmith2003]. The exclusion worry here has its own name, "pleiotropy", one gene working through many pathways, and modern practice is largely a battery of partial defenses against it [@davies2018].

Economics has made instrumental variables its house specialty, above all for evaluating policies. The classic is Angrist and Krueger's quarter-of-birth instrument: compulsory-schooling laws force children born early in the year to stay in school slightly longer, and that sliver of law-induced schooling instruments the effect of education on earnings [@angrist1991]. The Oregon Health Insurance Experiment, which @sec-rq-to-interpretation introduced, is a modern policy example: the lottery is the randomized instrument, Medicaid enrollment the treatment it moves, and the division you did there is the IV estimate of Medicaid's effect on health and finances [@finkelstein2012; @baicker2013]. In the Moving to Opportunity experiment, families in high-poverty housing projects were randomized to receive housing vouchers, but only some moved; using the voucher as an instrument for moving, children who moved before age 13 earned 31 percent more as adults than controls, a finding that reshaped American housing policy [@chetty2016]. And a design now common in applied economics uses institutional randomness as the instrument: in Norway, criminal cases are assigned to judges of measurably different strictness, so the assigned judge's leniency instruments incarceration itself; incarceration turned out to *reduce* reoffending, by 29 percentage points over five years, where the naive comparison had suggested the opposite [@bhuller2020].

Each of these designs inherits the three conditions in its own form, and the standard criticisms of instrumental variables are those conditions pressed hard. Economists learned that celebrated instruments can be weak; the quarter-of-birth instrument is the canonical case [@bound1995]. A subtler criticism: even a valid instrument answers a narrower question than the one usually asked, because it estimates the effect among "compliers", the units the instrument actually moved, and critics like @deaton2010 ask whether that local effect was the question anyone posed. Mediation analysis in psychology has its own list of criticisms: mediators measured minutes before outcomes, assumptions unstated, and a literature of causal-sounding conclusions resting on the naive $\beta$ path [@bullock2010; @rohrer2022]. The remedy is to keep the how-question but treat the mediation model as this book treats every model: as a set of assumptions waiting for a design.

## Mediation over time: the Yang model on panel data

Time is a design resource for mediation. A mediation theory is a claim about a process: the cause changes the mediator, and the changed mediator later changes the outcome. Measuring the three variables in that order, in separate waves of a panel, does two things at once. It secures part of failure one, because an arrow running backwards in time is absurd for the same reason an arrow into a coin flip is. And it takes the theory's own dynamics seriously: when the true process unfolds over time, cross-sectional mediation estimates are not just imprecise but systematically biased for the longitudinal parameters they are read as [@maxwell2007], and the standard repair is to measure the cause, the mediator, and the outcome at successive waves [@cole2003]. What temporal ordering does *not* buy is anything about failure two: nobody randomized the mediator in a panel either, and unmeasured common causes of mediator and outcome are as dangerous across waves as within one.

The LISS panel repeats both questionnaires of @sec-theory-to-glm every year, so the full Yang model can be taken to panel data. Three annual waves (2023, 2024, 2025) give the temporally ordered version: social integration in 2023, the two measurable physiological states, hypertension and BMI, in 2024, and the count of other diagnosed conditions in 2025, with the states' disturbances correlated and, as the theory demands, no direct path from integration to disease.^[The analysis file is built from waves 16-18 of the LISS Health and Social Integration studies by `analysis/liss/03-longitudinal-yang.R` in the book's repository, with the same variable construction as @sec-theory-to-glm in every wave. The models use full-information maximum likelihood, so all 6,616 adults observed in at least one wave contribute.]

```{r}
#| label: liss-long-m3
#| warning: false
library(lavaan)
liss <- readRDS("../data/liss-health-social-integration/liss_yang_longitudinal.rds")
m3 <- "
  hypertension_17  ~ g1 * integration_16
  bmi_17           ~ g2 * integration_16
  disease_count_18 ~ b1 * hypertension_17 + b2 * bmi_17
  hypertension_17 ~~ psi * bmi_17
"
fit3 <- sem(m3, data = liss, estimator = "MLR", missing = "fiml",
            fixed.x = FALSE)
fitMeasures(fit3, c("ntotal", "chisq.scaled", "df.scaled", "pvalue.scaled"))
standardizedSolution(fit3)[1:5, c("lhs", "op", "rhs", "est.std", "se", "pvalue")]
```

The exclusion restriction passes: one degree of freedom, chi-square 0.36, $p = .55$. The estimates say that integration in one year predicts lower BMI the next ($-.06$), that it barely touches the hypertension diagnosis, and that both states predict the later disease count (.29 and .10). A two-wave version, integration in 2024 predicting states and disease in 2025, gives nearly identical numbers. That should raise a suspicion rather than settle the matter: if putting a year between the variables changes nothing, perhaps the estimates were never about what happens over a year.

The suspicion can be tested by letting each variable control its own past, the longitudinal design of @cole2003:

```{r}
#| label: liss-long-m3ar
#| warning: false
m3ar <- "
  hypertension_17  ~ g1 * integration_16 + a1 * hypertension_16
  bmi_17           ~ g2 * integration_16 + a2 * bmi_16
  disease_count_18 ~ b1 * hypertension_17 + b2 * bmi_17 +
                     a3 * disease_count_16
  hypertension_17 ~~ psi * bmi_17
"
fit3ar <- sem(m3ar, data = liss, estimator = "MLR", missing = "fiml",
              fixed.x = FALSE)
s <- standardizedSolution(fit3ar)
s[s$op == "~", c("lhs", "rhs", "est.std", "se", "pvalue")]
```

Almost everything disappears. The autoregressive paths are enormous, .82 to .91, because a diagnosis, once given, stays: these outcomes are cumulative stocks, and year-to-year change in them is rare. What is left after controlling the past is the model's answer to a different and better-matched question, whether integration predicts *changes* in the states and whether those changes predict *changes* in disease. The answer is: barely. Integration still predicts BMI change ($-.019$, small but reliable), the state-change paths shrink to .05 and .03, and the total indirect effect falls from $-.008$ to about $-.001$. In other words, most of what the first model reported was stable between-person differences described twice, not a process caught in the act, which is precisely the bias @maxwell2007 warned that cross-sectional habits of reading impose on longitudinal questions.

Two further results from the fuller analysis are worth carrying forward.^[The complete set of models, including the two-wave version, is in `analysis/liss/liss-longitudinal-report.md` in the book's repository.] First, adding age and sex to the three-wave model uncovers the suppression pattern of @sec-theory-to-glm again: integration's path to hypertension, invisible in the raw model, emerges at $-.034$ ($p = .016$) once age is held constant, because age raises both organizational involvement and blood pressure. Second, with the controls in place the exclusion test itself sharpens to a borderline rejection ($\chi^2(1) = 4.6$, $p = .03$), while the freed direct path stays small and nonsignificant. A test with nothing to explain is easy to pass; the same restriction under a better-specified model has more work to do, and its verdict becomes correspondingly more informative.

::: {.callout-tip icon="false" title="Exercise 3.6"}
(a) In the three-wave model the exclusion restriction passes with $\chi^2(1) = 0.36$. Why is this only weak support for the theory's claim that integration reaches disease only through the body?
(b) The autoregressive controls reduced every structural path by a factor of five or more. What feature of the outcome measures is responsible, and why does it matter for mediation specifically?
(c) Suppose integration's effect on physiology takes a decade to accumulate. What would the models of this section find, and what does that imply about the choice of lag?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false" title="Answer 3.6"}
(a) A restriction is informative only when it could have failed. Integration's correlations with the disease count are close to zero in these data, so there is almost nothing for the missing direct path to explain, and nearly any model omitting it would fit. The chi-square tests the restriction given the association present; with the age-adjusted model, where the association has structure, the same restriction is nearly rejected.
(b) Hypertension and the disease count record whether a condition was *ever* diagnosed, so they can only stay level or rise, and their year-to-year stability is .82-.91. Controlling the previous wave removes all of that stable variance, leaving only new diagnoses within one year, which are rare. Mediation is a claim about transmitted *change*, so the change-based estimates are the ones the claim is about; the uncontrolled estimates largely re-describe stable differences between people.
(c) The one-year-lag paths would be nearly zero even if the theory were true, because the model looks for the effect at the wrong interval. Longitudinal effects are functions of the lag at which they are measured, and a nonsignificant lagged path is evidence against the mechanism only at that lag. Choosing the lag is a theoretical decision that the data cannot make by themselves.
:::

## Modern mediation analysis, briefly

@sec-theory-to-glm left a question open. When the arrow into the mediator carries an ordinary regression coefficient and the arrow out of it carries a log-odds coefficient, as in the published diagram of @bayerl2024, the product of the two multiplies numbers on different scales and means nothing in particular. Here is the answer. The framework above is linear; real mediation problems bring binary outcomes, interactions, and nonlinearity, and for those the modern literature defines the effects counterfactually before estimating anything [@vanderweele2016]. This literature has its own notation, which we adopt for this section: $X$ is the treatment, $M$ the mediator, $Y$ the outcome; $M(x)$ is the mediator value a person would have under treatment level $x$, and $Y(x, m)$ the outcome they would have under treatment $x$ with the mediator set to $m$.

Two definitions are worth knowing, because applied papers run on them. The **natural direct effect** compares the outcome under treatment versus control while the mediator is held at the value it would naturally take under control,

$$\text{NDE} = E[\,Y(1, M(0)) - Y(0, M(0))\,],$$

the effect that does not run through the mediator. The **natural indirect effect** holds treatment fixed and compares the outcome under the mediator value it would take with treatment versus without,

$$\text{NIE} = E[\,Y(1, M(1)) - Y(1, M(0))\,],$$

the effect that does run through the mediator. Adding the two makes the middle terms cancel, leaving $E[Y(1, M(1)) - Y(0, M(0))]$: the total effect, a decomposition as tidy as the linear one. In the linear model without interactions the NIE is exactly the coefficient product of this chapter's first section. As soon as the model departs from that form, the classic product and the counterfactual definitions part ways, and the counterfactual ones are right.

The smallest departure already shows it. Suppose treatment is 0 or 1 and the fitted equations are

$$
M = 0.5\,X + \zeta_M, \qquad
Y = 0.2\,X + 0.3\,M + 0.4\,XM + \zeta_Y,
$$

an ordinary mediation model plus one interaction term: the mediator matters more for treated units (0.3 + 0.4 = 0.7) than for controls (0.3). The classic product multiplies the treatment's effect on the mediator by the mediator's coefficient: $0.5 \times 0.3 = 0.15$. The counterfactual calculation asks instead what actually happens through the mediator when a unit is treated. Treatment raises the mediator by $E[M(1)] - E[M(0)] = 0.5$; for a treated unit, each unit of mediator is worth $0.3 + 0.4 = 0.7$; so $\text{NIE} = 0.5 \times 0.7 = 0.35$, more than twice the classic answer. (The NDE here is $0.2 + 0.4 \times E[M(0)] = 0.2$ when the untreated mediator averages zero, and $0.35 + 0.2 = 0.55$ is the total effect.) The classic product is not wrong arithmetic; it is the right answer to a question the model no longer asks, because with the interaction present there is no longer any single "effect of the mediator" to multiply by.

The R package `mediation` computes these effects by simulation for a wide menu of models [@tingley2014], under the same no-confounding assumptions you met above, there called "sequential ignorability". A classic demonstration uses a framing experiment: participants were randomized to an anxiety-inducing immigration news story, with anxiety as the mediator and sending an anti-immigration letter to Congress as the binary outcome [@brader2008].

```{r}
#| label: brader
#| cache: true
library(mediation)
data(framing)
med.fit <- lm(emo ~ treat + age + educ + gender + income, data = framing)
out.fit <- glm(cong_mesg ~ emo + treat + age + educ + gender + income,
               data = framing, family = binomial("probit"))
set.seed(1)
med.out <- mediate(med.fit, out.fit, treat = "treat", mediator = "emo",
                   robustSE = TRUE, sims = 1000)
round(summary(med.out)$d.avg, 3)   # average causal mediation effect (NIE)
round(summary(med.out)$z.avg, 3)   # average direct effect (NDE)
```

The first model explains the mediator, the second the outcome; `mediate()` combines them into the average causal mediation effect (the NIE, here about 0.08 and significant) and the average direct effect (small and not significant). The treatment raised the probability of writing to Congress by about eight percentage points *through anxiety*. Because the identifying assumptions are untestable, careful papers add a sensitivity analysis, which asks how strong an unmeasured mediator-outcome confounder would have to be to explain the result away; the package computes this too, and current reporting guidelines ask for exactly such statements.

A closing word on standard errors, because the mediation literature is oddly obsessed with them. The indirect effect $\gamma_1\beta$ is a product of two estimates, and `lavaan`'s `:=` operator gives its standard error by the delta method in one line. Bootstrapping, which is discussed in subsequent chapters, gives nearly the same answer at ordinary sample sizes.^[The product of two normal estimates is not itself normal, which matters near zero and in small samples [@mackinnon2007]; the bootstrap handles this and is a fine tool.]

## Reading the chapter backwards

Identification is a property of the question-design pair. It does not belong to the estimator, and neither sample size nor software can supply it. The mediation story taught each general lesson in miniature. Two opposite models fit identically, so data cannot orient an edge the design did not orient. A hidden confounder made every estimate precise and wrong, because assumptions the design does not support fail silently. One untestable assumption, exclusion, restored identification: what the data cannot supply, assumptions must, and the design determines how plausible those assumptions are. Panel data restored part of the causal order, while leaving the confounding problem and the choice of lag untouched. And the instrument's own conditions moved the limits rather than abolishing them. When you meet an analysis, any analysis, ask the fifth of the five questions of @sec-rq-to-interpretation with maximal severity: what in the design put the answer to this question into the data at all? If none did, no estimator will get it out. Mediation analysis is an if-then statement: if the assumptions hold, then this is the mediation process. Papers that claim mediation because the model said so are walking in a circle.

## Test yourself {.unnumbered}

::: {.callout-tip icon="false" title="Exercise 3.A"}
An abstract reads: "Whether living near a fast-food outlet causes obesity is disputed, since outlets choose their locations. We exploit the fact that highway service areas host fast-food outlets for reasons unrelated to local residents' health. Among 130,000 residents of towns at varying distances from service areas, we use highway proximity as an instrument for fast-food exposure and estimate its effect on body mass index."

(a) Identify the three variables in the instrumental-variable triangle and draw the assumed diagram, including the correlated disturbances.
(b) Write the three implied correlations and derive the IV estimator of the exposure effect.
(c) Suppose highway proximity also brings traffic noise and air pollution, which affect health. Which condition fails, and what happens to the estimate?
(d) Suppose fast-food outlets near highways serve the same food as elsewhere, but residents near highways rarely eat out at all, so proximity barely shifts exposure. Which condition fails, and what happens to the estimate?
(e) A colleague proposes to fix problem (c) by controlling for measured air quality. What assumption does the fix require?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false" title="Answer 3.A"}
(a) $\xi$ = highway proximity (instrument), $\eta_1$ = fast-food exposure, $\eta_2$ = BMI; arrows $\xi \rightarrow \eta_1 \rightarrow \eta_2$, curved arrow between the disturbances of $\eta_1$ and $\eta_2$, no direct $\xi \rightarrow \eta_2$ path. (b) $\rho_{\xi\eta_1} = \gamma_1$, $\rho_{\xi\eta_2} = \gamma_1\beta$, $\rho_{\eta_1\eta_2} = \beta + \text{confounding}$; hence $\beta = \rho_{\xi\eta_2}/\rho_{\xi\eta_1}$. (c) Exclusion: pollution and noise are direct paths from proximity to BMI that bypass exposure, so $\rho_{\xi\eta_2} = \gamma_1\beta + \text{direct part}$ and the ratio no longer isolates $\beta$; the estimate absorbs the pollution effect. (d) Relevance: $\gamma_1 \approx 0$, the denominator is near zero, and the estimator becomes wildly unstable (and any small exclusion violation is amplified). (e) That air quality is measured well enough, and that after controlling for it no *other* direct path from proximity to BMI remains; the exclusion restriction is repaired only as far as the controls are complete, which is an assumption, not a test result.
:::

::: {.callout-tip icon="false" title="Exercise 3.B"}
A published paper reports, from a cross-sectional survey of 2,000 office workers: "Job insecurity predicted burnout ($\beta = 0.21$). This effect was fully mediated by sleep quality ($ab = 0.19$, bootstrap 95% CI [0.12, 0.27]); the direct effect was not significant. We conclude that insecure employment burns people out by disrupting their sleep, and that sleep interventions can undo this harm."

(a) List the assumptions this conclusion requires, and label each as supported or unsupported by the design.
(b) Construct a concrete rival world, with the same fitted numbers, in which sleep interventions would achieve nothing.
(c) The authors emphasize the bootstrap confidence interval. Evaluate, in one or two sentences, how much that emphasis adds.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false" title="Answer 3.B"}
(a) Correct causal order (insecurity $\rightarrow$ sleep $\rightarrow$ burnout): unsupported; all three variables were measured at once, and burnt-out workers may sleep badly and read their job prospects more darkly. No insecurity-sleep confounding and no sleep-burnout confounding: unsupported; a failing employer, say, plausibly causes insecurity, late nights, and exhaustion at once. Linearity and additivity: conventional. (b) Let the employer's decline drive insecurity, poor sleep, and burnout, with no arrow from sleep to burnout at all: the three correlations can reproduce the published coefficients, yet improving sleep changes nothing because sleep never caused the burnout. (c) Very little. The bootstrap gives a valid interval around $ab$, but the number it brackets is causal only under the assumptions in (a); a precise confidence interval around an unidentified quantity is precision about the wrong thing.
:::

::: {.callout-tip icon="false" title="Exercise 3.C"}
A Mendelian randomization study uses a variant that slows alcohol metabolism as an instrument for alcohol consumption, with esophageal cancer as the outcome.

(a) State the three instrument conditions in genetic terms.
(b) The variant also causes facial flushing, which affects social behaviour and stress; through which condition does this threaten the analysis, and what is the term of art?
(c) The variant is common in East Asian populations and rare elsewhere, and populations differ in diet. Explain the resulting bias and one design remedy.
(d) In what precise sense does even a successful analysis answer a "local" question?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false" title="Answer 3.C"}
(a) Relevance: the variant shifts consumption. Exogeneity: the variant is dealt independently of confounders of drinking and cancer, the meiotic lottery. Exclusion: the variant affects cancer only through consumption. (b) Exclusion; a second pathway from gene to outcome is "pleiotropy". (c) Ancestry is a common cause of carrying the variant and of dietary exposures: confounding of the instrument itself, called population stratification. Remedies: analyse within genetically homogeneous groups, adjust for genetic principal components, or use within-family designs, where the lottery argument holds exactly. (d) The estimate reflects the effect of consumption among people whose drinking the variant actually shifts, the compliers; heavy drinkers who would drink regardless contribute nothing, so extrapolation to them is an extra assumption [@angrist1996; @deaton2010].
:::
